opus-5.5.text:
I think the ideal is that you shouldn't have to think about which mode you're in. Right now people bounce between a quick chat, a deep research task, an agent that goes off and uses a browser, maybe voice when they're on the go. Those feel like separate products, but from the user's side it's one intent: "help me get this thing done."

So a unified experience should be able to infer how much effort a request deserves. If you ask a quick factual question, you want an answer in a second or two. If you ask something that really needs twenty minutes of searching and synthesizing, the model should recognize that, maybe check in with a clarifying question, and then go do the work asynchronously and come back to you. The interaction pattern changes, but you didn't have to pick it from a dropdown.

The other piece is continuity. Context should carry across those modes. If I started something by voice in the car, I should be able to pick it up on my laptop, see what the agent did, and steer it. And for the longer-running stuff, trust and transparency matter a lot. You want to see what it's doing, interrupt it, and have it ask for confirmation before anything consequential, like buying something or sending an email on your behalf.

So I'd say: one place, one memory of you and your task, and the model adapts the form of the interaction, whether that's fast, slow, synchronous, or in the background, to what you actually need, rather than making you learn a bunch of different tools.

r001.rationale: The response describes chat, research, browser-agent, and voice modes, but does not mention an encompassing ChatGPT experience alongside context-specific modes such as inline code completion.

r002.rationale: It says users should be able to interrupt and steer the agent, but does not state that interruption lets them correct the model’s interpretation of their intent.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose letting users take over from the model and type content themselves.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because the way you interact with a model really depends on what you're trying to do. Sometimes you want something back in a few seconds, you just have a quick question, and you want the model to answer immediately. And sometimes you have a task where you'd actually be happy to wait five minutes, or even longer, if it means the answer is much more thorough and you don't have to go back and forth.

So I don't think the right answer is one mode that's forced on everyone. I think the ideal experience is one where you can just say what you want, and the system figures out how much effort to spend. If the question is simple, it answers right away. If it's something like, "do a deep dive on this market and come back with a report," it should go off, browse, read a lot of sources, synthesize them, and come back with something well-cited. And it should probably tell you up front, "this is going to take a few minutes," so you can go do something else.

The other thing is that the interaction shouldn't end when the model starts working. For longer tasks, the model should be able to ask you clarifying questions before it starts, because that's often where things go wrong. If I'm asking for research, there's usually some ambiguity in what I actually want, and a quick clarification at the beginning saves a lot of wasted effort. And when it comes back, you should be able to keep the conversation going: ask follow-ups, say "actually, focus more on this part," and have it refine the work rather than starting from scratch.

So to me, unified means the user doesn't have to think about which tool or model to pick. You just express your intent, and the right amount of reasoning, tool use, and time gets allocated behind the scenes. We're not fully there yet, but I think that's where things are headed.

r001.rationale: The response describes quick and long-running tasks in a unified experience, but does not propose both a conversational experience and context-specific modes such as inline code completion.

r002.rationale: It proposes clarifying questions before work and follow-ups after it returns, but does not say users can interrupt the model while it is working to correct its interpretation.

r003.rationale: The response discusses asking follow-ups and refining the model's work, but does not propose users taking over and typing content themselves.

astra-6.text:
I think a unified experience should let you move really naturally between different ways of interacting with the model. Sometimes I want to type something, sometimes I want to talk, and sometimes I want to show it what I’m looking at. Those shouldn’t feel like separate products where I have to start over and explain all the context again.

And then there’s how involved I want to be. For some tasks, I want a very quick answer. For others, I want to go back and forth and work through something together. And sometimes I want to hand off a task and come back when it needs my input or has a result. I think the experience should accommodate all of those, while making it clear what the model is doing and giving me an easy way to steer it.

r001.rationale: The response describes moving between typing, talking, and showing the model things, but does not propose an encompassing chat experience alongside context-specific modes such as inline code completion.

r002.rationale: It mentions an easy way to steer the model, but does not clearly propose interrupting it to correct its interpretation of the user's intent.

r003.rationale: The response mentions typing as one way to interact, but does not propose taking over from the model and typing content oneself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a unified experience has to recognize that you want different levels of involvement for different tasks. Sometimes I want to ask a quick question and get an answer. Sometimes I want to work with the model, going back and forth on something. And sometimes I want to delegate a task and come back when it’s done.

Those should feel like different ways of interacting with the same system. It should have the relevant context, let me move between those modes easily, and make it clear when it needs my input. The interface can adapt to the task without making me figure out which model or tool I’m supposed to use.

r001.rationale: The response describes quick questions, back-and-forth work, and delegation within one system, but does not propose both a broad conversational experience and context-specific modes such as inline code completion.

r002.rationale: It says the system should make clear when it needs the user's input, but does not propose interrupting it to correct its interpretation of the user's intent.

r003.rationale: The response mentions moving between interaction modes, but does not propose letting users take over and type content themselves.
